svg.aria-label: AWS Lambda functions now support full IAM resource-based policies: a comparison of AddPermission, which writes one Allow statement at a time with only three condition keys, against PutResourcePolicy, which takes a complete JSON document supporting explicit Deny and the full range of IAM condition keys; a warning that PutResourcePolicy replaces the entire existing policy including statements AWS services added when triggers were configured; how a cross-account invoke is evaluated in both accounts; and the two budgets the feature spends, a 20 KB policy size and a 15 request per second control plane rate
svg.title: AWS Lambda functions now support full IAM resource-based policies. Until now a function policy was assembled one AddPermission call at a time: every statement was an Allow, one principal per call, and only three condition keys were available, namely aws:SourceArn, aws:SourceAccount and aws:PrincipalOrgID. AddPermission appends to the existing policy without overwriting it, and it is what the Lambda console writes when you add a trigger and what AWS::Lambda::Permission emits in CloudFormation, SAM and CDK. The new PutResourcePolicy operation takes one complete JSON document, supporting Allow and explicit Deny, multiple principals and actions in a single statement, and the complete range of IAM global condition keys, with optimistic concurrency through a RevisionId, and it is refused with a PublicPolicyException if the policy would grant public access. The hazard is that PutResourcePolicy replaces the entire existing policy, including every statement that Amazon S3, Amazon EventBridge, Amazon API Gateway and Amazon SNS added through AddPermission when their triggers were configured, so one call can silently stop every trigger firing. Retrieve the current policy with GetResourcePolicy first, merge, and pass the RevisionId so that a concurrent change fails with HTTP 412 rather than disappearing. A cross-account invocation is evaluated in both accounts: the identity policy in the trusted account must allow the call and the resource policy in the trusting account must allow the principal, and the request is allowed only if both evaluations return Allow, while an explicit Deny in either one ends it. That is why a Deny in the function policy is worth having, because it reaches callers whose identity policies you do not own. The two budgets the feature spends are a function resource-based policy quota of 20 KB, which is 20,480 bytes for the whole document, and a Lambda control plane rate of 15 requests per second across all APIs, which cannot be increased.

g.text: A Lambda function finally has a policy, not a pile of permissions
The capability is welcome. The call that delivers it replaces everything already there, including what AWS wrote for you.
1. Two ways to write the same policy, and only one of them can say no
AddPermission — one Allow statement at a time
Effect is always Allow. There is no way to express a Deny.
One principal per call. Ten principals means ten calls.
Three condition keys only: aws:SourceArn, aws:SourceAccount
and aws:PrincipalOrgID.
Appends without overwriting. This is what the console writes
for a trigger, and what AWS::Lambda::Permission emits.
PutResourcePolicy — one complete JSON document
Allow and explicit Deny. Sid, Condition, multiple principals
and multiple actions in a single statement.
The complete range of IAM global condition keys.
RevisionId gives you optimistic concurrency, if you pass it.
Refused with PublicPolicyException if the policy would grant
public access. Replaces whatever was there before.
2. That last line is the whole post: put-resource-policy replaces the policy, all of it
Your function has six statements on it. Five of them you did not write.
Amazon S3 added one when you set the bucket notification. EventBridge added one for the rule. API Gateway added one per stage.
Amazon SNS added one for the topic. Each arrived through AddPermission, appended quietly, and appears in none of your templates.
One put-resource-policy call replaces all six with whatever you sent. Nothing warns you. The triggers simply stop firing.
Read first with get-resource-policy, merge, and send the RevisionId back so a concurrent change fails with HTTP 412 instead of vanishing.
3. A cross-account invoke is evaluated twice, which is what makes a Deny here worth writing
Trusted account A calls the function in trusting account B
A’s identity policy must allow lambda:InvokeFunction on the function ARN. B’s resource policy must allow the principal in A.
AWS evaluates both accounts and allows the request only if both evaluations return Allow. An explicit Deny in either one ends it.
So a Deny on the function reaches callers whose identity policies you do not own, cannot read, and were never going to audit.
4. The two budgets this feature spends
Neither is adjustable, and the second one is the reason a fleet-wide rollout takes longer than you planned.
Function resource-based policy
20 KB — 20,480 bytes for the whole document, every statement included
Lambda control plane API rate
15 requests per second across all APIs, not per API, and not increasable
Available in all AWS commercial Regions at no additional charge. Existing AddPermission policies continue to work without modification.
